summary: Roy Derks, an IBM engineer with a startup and GraphQL background, argues tool calling deserves far more attention than it receives. While the AI community focuses on agent frameworks and LLM capabilities, tools—where things most often break—are neglected. Derks believes tools should be reusable, robust, and separable from agentic frameworks, giving developers flexibility to switch frameworks. He frames the principle as the agent is only as good as its tools. He recaps tool calling using a moon-orbit example and explains that a good tool definition includes a simple name, a rich description functioning like a system prompt, input parameters, and increasingly an output schema for type safety and tool-call chaining. He distinguishes traditional tool calling (explicit callbacks, error/retry handling, manual orchestration) from embedded tool calling (closed-system black box where tools go in and answers come out). Embedded tool calling is easy for beginners but offers no control over execution, error handling, or decision-making. As a longtime developer, Derks strongly prefers separation of concerns. He sees MCP (Model Context Protocol), introduced by Anthropic, as a major step forward—it separates the host/client from servers that handle tool logic and data access. Beyond MCP, he highlights standalone tool platforms (e.g., IBM's WX Flow, Compos, Tool House, Arcade AI, Wild Card) where tools are created and executed independently, then imported into any agentic framework via SDKs or API calls. This lets developers build tools once and use them across LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, or LangGraph. These platforms also handle tool chaining, authorization, authentication, and error management. Derks then addresses dynamic tools using GraphQL and SQL: instead of creating many fixed tools (which confuse agents at scale—around 100 tools), developers can provide a GraphQL schema and let the LLM generate valid queries. Models understand GraphQL features like fragments, but schemas should avoid deep nesting (one level is fine, five is confusing) and custom scalars. Dynamic tools reduce downstream implementation by eliminating the need to define 20 separate tools and duplicate business logic. However, trade-offs include hallucination risk and inconsistent syntax generation. Derks sees a strong future for dynamic tools over static ones and closes by reiterating that tools are as important as the agents themselves.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Roy Derks introduces the talk on tool calling for AI agents, outlines what will be covered (traditional vs meta tool calling, agent frameworks, tool platforms), and shares his background in startups, GraphQL, and IBM.

sections.title: Why tools deserve more attention
sections.summary: Derks argues people focus on agents but neglect tools, which break first. He advocates for reusable, robust, framework-agnostic tools and states the agent is only as good as its tools. The application layer must catch up as LLMs improve.

sections.title: Tool calling recap and tool definition
sections.summary: Uses a moon-orbit-as-trips example to recap tool calling. Explains tool definition components: simple name, rich description (like a system prompt), input parameters, and output schema for type safety and chaining. Mentions dynamic tools with GraphQL and SQL.

sections.title: Traditional vs embedded tool calling
sections.summary: Contrasts traditional tool calling (explicit callback functions, error/retry handling, manual orchestration between client and server) with embedded tool calling (closed-system black box where tools go in and answers come out). References LangChain and IBM watsonx examples.

sections.title: Embedded tool calling limitations and separation of concerns
sections.summary: Expands on embedded tool calling as a black box where tools go in and answers come out. Easy for beginners but no control over execution, errors, retries, or decision-making. Derks advocates for separation of concerns, drawing parallels to his PHP/Laravel experience and the desire to separate backends from frontends.

sections.title: MCP and standalone tool platforms
sections.summary: Introduces MCP (Model Context Protocol) from Anthropic as a way to separate host/client from tool servers. Then discusses standalone tool platforms (WX Flow, Compos, Tool House, Arcade AI, Wild Card) where tools are created and executed independently, imported into any agentic framework via SDKs. Enables building tools once and switching frameworks easily. Platforms handle chaining, authorization, and errors.

sections.title: Tool platform integration example and dynamic tools
sections.summary: Shows a WX Flow integration with LangGraph react agent, demonstrating how tools are pulled from a remote platform while the agent remains a black box. Then introduces dynamic tools using GraphQL schemas: instead of many fixed tools, the model generates valid GraphQL queries from a provided schema. Notes that around 100 tools confuses agents, and custom GraphQL scalars should be avoided for model-generated queries.

sections.title: Dynamic tools best practices, trade-offs, and closing
sections.summary: Covers best practices for dynamic GraphQL tools: avoid deep nesting (one level is fine, five is confusing), models understand features like fragments. Dynamic tools reduce downstream implementation by eliminating need to define 20 separate tools and duplicate business logic. Trade-offs include hallucination risk and inconsistent syntax generation. Derks sees a strong future for dynamic over static tools and closes by reiterating tools are as important as the agents being built.
